title: Scikit-learn Reference
description: A quick reminder of the ideas and examples in the Scikit-learn lessons. Open the linked lesson when you need more help.

entries.name: Features and labels
entries.summary: A feature is an input measurement. A label is the known answer in a teaching example. Scikit-learn usually expects a table of feature rows.
notes: Do not give a different number of feature rows and labels.

entries.name: Fit a simple classifier
entries.summary: A classifier chooses a group label. fit lets the model learn from examples. A decision tree splits inputs using learned thresholds.

example.code:
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
X = [[1], [2], [8], [9]]
y = [0, 0, 1, 1]
model = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=1, random_state=0)
model.fit(X, y)
print(model.predict([[1.5], [8.5]]).tolist())

notes: A toy split does not prove a model will work on a real-world problem.

entries.name: Keep test data separate
entries.summary: A test set holds examples kept out of model fitting. It gives a better check than only asking about examples the model already saw.

example.code:
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
X = [[n] for n in range(10)]
y = [0] * 5 + [1] * 5
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2, random_state=0, stratify=y)
print(len(X_train), len(X_test))

notes: Repeatedly choosing changes based on test results can leak information from the test set.

entries.name: Use a simple baseline
entries.summary: A baseline is a simple result to compare against. DummyClassifier can always choose the most frequent training class.

example.code:
from sklearn.dummy import DummyClassifier
model = DummyClassifier(strategy="most_frequent")
model.fit([[1], [2], [3]], [0, 0, 1])
print(model.predict([[8], [9]]).tolist())

notes: Beating no comparison at all is not strong evidence; start with a simple baseline.

entries.name: Measure accuracy
entries.summary: Accuracy is the fraction of labels predicted correctly. It can be misleading when one class is much more common than another.
notes: Do not rely only on accuracy for rare but important outcomes.

entries.name: Read a confusion matrix
entries.summary: A confusion matrix counts correct and incorrect class choices. With labels [0, 1], rows are true labels and columns are predicted labels.

example.code:
from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix
print(confusion_matrix([0, 0, 1, 1], [0, 1, 1, 1], labels=[0, 1]).tolist())

notes: Check row and column meanings before interpreting a matrix.

entries.name: Scale using training data
entries.summary: Scaling puts features on a chosen numeric scale. Fit the scaler on training data, then use that fitted scaler on other data.

example.code:
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
scaler = StandardScaler()
scaled = scaler.fit_transform([[1.0], [2.0], [3.0]])
print(round(float(scaled[1, 0]), 6))

notes: Fitting the scaler on all data before splitting leaks test information.

entries.name: Pipelines keep steps together
entries.summary: A pipeline applies preparation and a model in the intended order. It helps use the same preparation for fitting and prediction.

example.code:
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
model = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=1))
model.fit([[1], [2], [8], [9]], [0, 0, 1, 1])
print(model.predict([[1.5], [8.5]]).tolist())

notes: Do not manually apply a second, different scaling step to predictions.

entries.name: Predict a number with regression
entries.summary: Regression predicts a number instead of a class. LinearRegression fits a straight-line relationship to the examples.

example.code:
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
model = LinearRegression().fit([[1], [2], [3]], [2, 4, 6])
print(round(float(model.predict([[4]])[0]), 2))

notes: A real dataset may not follow a perfect straight line.

entries.name: Measure numeric error
entries.summary: Mean absolute error averages the size of prediction mistakes without keeping their plus or minus signs.
notes: The error is in the target's units; do not compare unrelated tasks without context.

entries.name: Cross-validation repeats a check
entries.summary: Cross-validation trains and evaluates on several train/validation splits. It gives more than one estimate, but still needs careful data grouping.

example.code:
from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score
X, y = load_iris(return_X_y=True)
scores = cross_val_score(DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=2, random_state=0), X, y, cv=3)
print(len(scores))

notes: Related records from the same person or future time must not leak across splits.

entries.name: Inspect the model limit
entries.summary: A model setting chosen before fitting is a hyperparameter. max_depth limits how many splits a tree can make along a path.

example.code:
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
model = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=1, random_state=0)
model.fit([[1], [2], [8], [9]], [0, 0, 1, 1])
print(model.get_depth())

notes: More complex models can memorise training details instead of learning useful patterns.
